title: proc extension: background process manager for pi

notes.content: User agreed: survive reload/new/resume/fork; stop all on quit; no restart-reattach in v1.

children.question: What happens to running processes when pi reloads / starts a new session / quits?
children.answer: Processes are owned by the pi process. They survive `/reload`, `/new`, `/resume`, and `/fork` (state kept on a `globalThis` symbol and listeners rebound), but on pi `quit` the extension stops every running process (SIGTERM the group, then SIGKILL after a timeout). Rationale: after pi exits we can no longer capture stdout/stderr, so a "surviving" process would be unmanageable and invisible. Restart-persistence/reattach is out of scope for v1.

notes.content: User agreed: detached process group, group kill, stop=SIGTERM->SIGKILL escalation, kill=SIGKILL, optional signal override.

children.question: How do we stop processes: process-group ownership, escalation, and stop vs kill semantics?
children.answer: Spawn each process in its own process group (`detached: true`) so we can signal the whole tree, and kill with `process.kill(-pid, sig)`. `stop` = SIGTERM the group, escalate to SIGKILL after ~3s. `kill` = SIGKILL the group immediately. Both accept an optional `signal` override (`SIGINT`, `SIGHUP`, `SIGTERM`, `SIGKILL`). No stdin magic (no writing `q`/`exit`) — that is what `write` is for. This prevents the classic orphaned-children case from `npm run dev`/`bash -lc`.

notes.content: User agreed: retained until forget or cap ~20 exited; status bar red for ~60s then drop.

children.question: How long do exited processes stick around (in list and in the status bar)?
children.answer: Keep exited processes in `list` and in memory until either `forget <name>` is called or the extension hits a cap of ~20 retained exited processes (oldest auto-dropped). Exited entries always have a `forget` path. On pi `quit` everything is cleared anyway. The status bar shows exited processes in red for ~60s after exit, then drops them from the bar (but they stay in `list` until forgotten).

notes.content: User agreed. Also agreed: run refuses a name that is still running; run replaces an exited name.

children.question: What is the exact `write` (stdin) behavior?
children.answer: `write` takes `name`, `input` (string), optional `newline` (default true), and optional `close` (default false, sends EOF/ends stdin). Stdin is opened as a pipe at spawn and kept open. `write` fails with a clear error if the process already exited or stdin is not writable. No shell-style escaping; the string goes through as-is (plus `\n` unless `newline:false`).

children.question: What happens if `run` is called with a name that already exists?
children.answer: `run` refuses to reuse a name whose process is still running (clear error). If the name belongs to an exited process, `run` replaces that entry.

notes.content: User agreed: both agent tool (primary) and user-facing /px:proc command; no shortcuts in v1.

children.question: Should the extension be agent-tool-only, or also expose user-facing slash commands (e.g. list/kill/tail a process by hand)?
children.answer: Both, but the agent tool is the primary interface. Expose a `proc` tool for the agent, plus a small user-facing `/px:proc` command (list + kill + view logs) for interactive control. No keyboard shortcuts in v1.

notes.content: User agreed: single umbrella `proc` tool with actions run/list/status/logs/stop/kill/write/forget.

children.question: Tool shape: one umbrella `proc` tool with an `action` enum, or several separate tools (`proc_run`, `proc_logs`, ...)?
children.answer: One umbrella tool named `proc` with an `action` enum: `run`, `list`, `status`, `logs`, `stop`, `kill`, `write`, `forget`. Fewer tools keeps the system prompt small, and actions share the same id/naming logic. Use StringEnum for action (Google compatibility).

notes.content: User agreed: run takes a shell command string via bash -lc, with optional cwd and env; no argv mode in v1.

children.question: How does `run` accept the process to start: a shell command string, or an argv array?
children.answer: `run` takes a single `command` shell string, executed as `bash -lc "<command>"` so pipes, env vars, and `&&` work. Optional `cwd` (defaults to `ctx.cwd`) and optional `env` map merged onto `process.env`. Do not use argv arrays in v1; the model naturally writes shell strings and it keeps the schema tiny.

notes.content: User agreed ('ok'): name is the id, derived from command, optional override, numeric suffixes for collisions.

children.question: How are processes identified and named (needed for the status bar short name)?
children.answer: The short name IS the id. Default derives from the command's first word basename (e.g. `npm run dev` -> `npm`, `./serve.sh` -> `serve`), sanitized to `[a-z0-9_-]`. Optional `name` param overrides it. Collisions get a numeric suffix (`vite`, `vite-2`). `run` returns the name and pid; every other action takes `name`. Names stay reserved after exit until `forget` (or a retention timeout, decided later).

notes.content: User agreed: list/status shapes as proposed; exit produces ui.notify + red status bar, no automatic agent message injection in v1.

children.question: What should `list`/`status` show, and how does the agent learn a process exited (notify/inject vs poll)?
children.answer: `list` returns all known processes as compact rows: name, state (`running`/`exited`), pid, uptime/duration, exit code or signal, and unread log lines. `status <name>` returns one process with command, cwd, start time, duration, exit detail, and the last ~20 log lines. Exited processes stay listed until `forget` or retention. On exit the extension shows a `ctx.ui.notify` (and status bar turns red); it does NOT inject a message into the agent conversation in v1, so the agent polls when it cares.

children.question: What is the exact /px:proc subcommand grammar?
children.answer: `/px:proc` grammar: bare `/px:proc` or `/px:proc list` shows all processes (notify text). `/px:proc logs <name> [lines]` tails the user-reader cursor (default 50); `/px:proc logs <name> --start [lines]` from the earliest retained line. `/px:proc stop <name>` and `/px:proc kill <name>` and `/px:proc forget <name>`. When `<name>` is omitted, use `ctx.ui.select` (running-only for stop/kill; all for logs/forget). No `/px:proc run` in v1 - users have `!` bash and the agent has the tool.

children.question: What is the log buffer model and the "since last read" cursor model?
children.answer: One ordered, line-based in-memory ring buffer per process, tagged out:/err: and preserving arrival order. Cap 5000 lines or 2 MB per process, whichever first; trims are counted and reported as `dropped`. Per-reader cursors: `agent` (tool calls) and `user` (/px:proc logs) advance independently. `logs { name, from: "last" | "start" }` where "last" (default) returns only lines after that reader's cursor and "start" returns from the earliest retained line. Responses include cursor, dropped, and running.

notes.content: User agreed: logs args/return as proposed, cursor advances only for from:last.

children.question: What are the exact `logs` arguments and return shape?
children.answer: `logs` args: `name`; `from` = `"last"` (default) | `"start"` | integer line number; `lines` = max lines to return (default 200, max 2000); `filter` = `"out" | "err"` optional. Response is a small header line (`proc=vite state=running pid=1234 cursor=812 dropped=0 more=true`) followed by the tagged lines. After a successful `logs`, the reader's cursor moves past the returned lines (even if truncated by `lines`, it stays at the last returned line, so the next `from:"last"` continues). Integer `from` does NOT move the cursor unless `from:"last"` was used.

children.question: How are raw process bytes normalized into log lines (ANSI, carriage returns, long lines)?
children.answer: Normalize each stored line: strip ANSI CSI/SGR/OSC escape sequences; convert `\r\n` and lone `\r` to `\n`; drop empty lines; truncate a single line at 4096 chars with a `…(+N)` marker; prefix `out:` / `err:`. Progress-bar spam is acceptable in v1 (bounded by the ring cap); collapsing repeated lines is deferred.

children.question: Should `logs` support waiting for new output (to avoid agent polling)?
children.answer: Yes, but opt-in: `logs{ ..., wait?: seconds }` with `wait` 0–30 (default 0). When >0 the call resolves as soon as at least one new line is available for that reader, or on timeout. Cancellable via the tool's abort signal. Default stays 0 so normal reads are instant.

children.question: How does the proc extension get a dedicated status-bar row: new generic rows contract, or reuse line 2?
children.answer: Extend `status-bar` with a generic extra-rows contract: `px:status-bar:row:set { id, content, order? }` and `px:status-bar:row:clear { id }`. Each registered row renders as its own footer line after the existing two lines, sorted by `order` then registration, and hidden while empty. `proc` publishes id `proc`. This is display-mode agnostic (works in both new and legacy) and reusable by other producers. status-bar README/contract must document it.

children.question: What exactly goes in the process row (format, dot colors, ordering, overflow)?
children.answer: Row format: one item per process, `● <name> <pid>`, items joined with `  ·  `; e.g. `● vite 48231  ·  ● npm 48255`. Dot is `●` colored via theme: running=success (green), stopping=warning (yellow), exited code 0=muted (gray), exited non-zero/signal=error (red). Running processes first, then recently-exited. Only running + exited-within-60s are shown; if the line overflows, drop the oldest items and append `+N more`.

children.question: How does proc behave if status-bar is missing?
children.answer: Reuse the `status-bar` availability handshake from `flutter`: on `session_start` send `px:status-bar:ping {id:"proc"}`; listen for `px:status-bar:pong`; if no pong within ~500ms and UI is present, `ui.notify(..., "warning")` once. `proc` works fully without status-bar - it only loses the row. Re-ping on session changes/commands.

notes.content: User chose option A (safe-mode classifier), 'good for now'. Revisit a generic approval event API only if more extensions need it.

Codebase finding: safe-mode intercepts all tool_call events (index.ts ~L1202) and decideToolCall treats unknown tools as confirm (policy.ts ~L592). READ_ONLY_TOOLS set + isReaderAllowed are the extension points.

children.question: How does proc integrate with safe-mode for approvals?
children.answer: No routing layer. safe-mode already intercepts every tool_call (its handler has no tool-name filter) and treats unknown tools as confirm, so proc is already gated. Centralize decisions by adding a proc classifier to safe-mode's policy, like git/sqlite/http: list/status/logs = read-only (auto-allow in reader/smart); run/write/stop/kill/forget = confirm. For `run`, re-validate the command string with safe-mode's existing bash classifier so read-only commands auto-allow, and so `run "rm -rf /"` is classified as mutating. Requires touching safe-mode/policy.ts (classifyProcToolCall + describeToolCall + tests) and documenting it. proc still works without safe-mode.

children.question: What are the resource limits and where does configuration live?
children.answer: Max 8 concurrently running processes (configurable). `run` at the cap fails with a clear "stop or forget a process" error. Global config in `~/.pi/agent/proc.json` with defaults: maxProcesses=8, logLines=5000, logBytes=2_000_000, exitedRetentionMs=60000, exitedCap=20, statusRow=true. No project-local config in v1 (avoids project-trust complexity). Env overrides not needed in v1. Each process gets its own log buffer, so worst case ~16MB at defaults.

children.question: What files/deliverables does this change touch?
children.answer: Deliver as `extensions/proc/{index.ts,README.md}` with no new npm deps. Also update: root `README.md` extension table (add proc, dep status-bar), `install` extension list (add proc right after status-bar), `status-bar/README.md` + `contract.ts` for the new row events, and `safe-mode/policy.ts` + `policy.test.ts` + `README.md` for the proc classifier. Follow repo conventions: globalThis state, ping/pong status-bar handshake, Conventional Commits.
